query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, self-healing silicide coating on the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will improve its mechanical integrity without significantly compromising its caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that exhibits a large caloric effect under applied magnetic or pressure fields but tends to crack and has poor structural integrity.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin silicide coating on the alloy via pack cementation at a moderate temperature (around 950 °C for 24 h).
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied prior to caloric cycling. The alloy is then subjected to applied-field (magnetic and/or pressure) and temperature conditions similar to those used for its caloric operation, ensuring that the coating is tested under realistic operational loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-layer silicide structure consisting of an outer MSi2 layer and an inner MSi layer, which can self-heal via the formation of oxide particles within emerging cracks.
generation.mechanism: The silicide coating acts as a mechanically robust, crack-bridging layer. Under thermal and mechanical cycling, minor cracks in the coating become filled by in situ oxidation products (akin to the (Zr,Hf)O2 in refractory HfNbTaTiZr systems), thereby arresting crack propagation while its thinness ensures minimal interference with the phase transitions responsible for the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength enhanced by an estimated 2–3× compared to the uncoated alloy) with a negligible change (less than a 10% reduction) in the caloric performance metrics.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows excellent caloric effects but suffers from cracking and low compressive strength under loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under operational conditions similar to those used in caloric studies (i.e., under applied-field and pressure cycles, within a temperature regime that does not alter the intended phase transformation), and without introducing rare-earth elements or additional foreign phases that might alter the caloric mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding whether the silicide coating, despite being thin, might subtly alter the surface energy or stress distribution in a way that could influence the transformation kinetics driving the caloric effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples. Subject one set to pack cementation under the specified conditions to form the silicide coating, while leaving the other as an uncoated control. Perform cyclic loading under identical applied magnetic/pressure fields and temperature conditions. Measure the compressive strength and monitor crack propagation using optical and electron microscopy. Simultaneously, evaluate the caloric response (e.g., by measuring the adiabatic temperature change and/or entropy change) for both sets.
measurements: Crack density and propagation via imaging
Adiabatic temperature change or entropy change as a measure of caloric performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (for instance, less than a 2× increase in compressive strength) or exhibit a caloric response reduction greater than 10% compared to the uncoated control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
